correctness_topical.explantion: Response b includes a factual error—claiming that process philosophy directly prompted a reevaluation of marriage definitions toward personal fulfillment, which the cited sources do not support. According to the hierarchy of failure, factual errors outweigh any misleading or irrelevant content. Response a only has misleading and irrelevant statements but no factual errors, so it is topically superior.

coherence_logical.explantion: Response a contains an internal contradiction—labeling a long‑standing, static prohibition of same‑sex marriage as a clear example of process philosophy, which emphasizes continual change—while also describing that stance as static. This fatal logical flaw outweighs its other issues. Response b, although suffering from structural and flow problems and some redundancy, does not contain any internal contradictions. According to the hierarchy of failure, the presence of an internal contradiction in a makes it the loser, so response b is superior in logical coherence.

coherence_stylistic.explantion: Response b is free of any reported tonal, complexity, perspective, or abrupt style issues, maintaining a uniform academic voice throughout. In contrast, response a exhibits both a tone clash (informal phrasing like "Fast-forward to 2000s") and a complexity mismatch (mixing colloquial language with dense academic terms). These medium‑severity flaws reduce its stylistic coherence, so b is the superior response.

coverage_broad.explantion: Both responses suffer from high‑severity failures: they each miss major aspects of process philosophy and lack contextual introduction. However, response b lists a wider variety of ways process philosophy is said to influence marriage (legal recognition, individualistic shifts, divorce trends, feminist critiques, de‑facto relationships), whereas response a is almost entirely limited to the U.S. same‑sex marriage legal history. This broader enumeration gives response b a comparatively better coverage of the topic despite the shared shortcomings.

coverage_deep.explantion: Both responses suffer from the highest‑severity failures (surface‑level treatment and missing mechanisms), but response b provides a broader set of concrete illustrations (e.g., acceptance of divorce, cohabitation, de‑facto relationships, feminist critiques) whereas response a mentions only the generic case of same‑sex marriage legalization. Under the Substance Test, the presence of more specific examples gives response b the edge in deep coverage.

consistency_internal.explantion: Both responses exhibit the same high‑severity internal‑consistency failures: each blends distinct scholarly viewpoints with the claim that process philosophy directly caused legal and social changes (Blurred Viewpoints/Conflation), each presents unresolved contradictions about why moral arguments against same‑sex marriage disappeared or why divorce rates rose without reconciling alternative explanations (Unresolved Conflict), and each portrays these causal links as universally accepted (False Consensus) while omitting proper citations (Attribution Failure). Because the nature and impact of the errors are essentially identical, neither response demonstrably distinguishes perspectives better than the other, leading to a tie.
